utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, who is your first witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Our first witness is Velimir Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you will now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Obradovic. Could you please give us your name and surname for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I am Velimir Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of September, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read this statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Today if you were to be asked the same questions, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the statement of Mr. Velimir Obradovic is 4D499, and I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, could you please tell the Trial Chamber briefly something about your military career and your education.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after I completed secondary technical school for mechanic engineers in Belgrade, I applied to the military technical academy in Rajlovac, Sarajevo, and was admitted. Upon completing the academy, I was assigned the position of second lieutenant at the Nis airport at the 161st air base. That is where I was commander of the staff air squad in Nis. At the airport of Nis, I spent ten years. In that period of time, in the Yugoslav People's Army, there was an active youth organization, as an independent organization related to the youth association of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, I think that will do. I think you can move on.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that during the course of my work there I realised that I had an affinity for political science, and it is due to that affinity that I applied to the higher political school in Belgrade and was admitted there as well. I completed this school in 1984. After graduation I was immediately deployed to a military political duty in the 492nd air base in Pristina, the Pristina airport, that is. That's where I spent four years. After that I was reassigned to the 285th air base in Ladjevci, Kraljevo, and was appointed Chief of Staff of the air base. That is to say that these were operations duties that I had. After that, I was reassigned to the command of the air corps in Nis, where I had military political duties and then also in the operations organ of the command of the air corps. This was in 1987, that's when I -- or rather, I beg your pardon, in 1989 I came to the command of the air corps in Nis. And parallel to my job, I started a graduate course at the higher military political school in Belgrade, where I later got my master's degree. After that, I became chief of the cabinet of the commander of the 3rd Army in 1992. I was chief of cabinet all the way up to the end of 1998. I had several army commanders there, from General Uzelac to General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Obradovic. Could you please now tell the Trial Chamber what duties you had in 1999.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1999, sometime in January, I was appointed chief of the operations centre of the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what your duties were as chief of operations centre of the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, my basic duty was to tap all human resources, space resources of the operations centre, and to make it possible for the operations duty team as the highest organ in the operations duty section in-depth of the 3rd Army to work efficiently, first of all; and secondly round the clock. According to all assessments made, this was indeed carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what were the duties of the operations centre in the period of time while you were chief of this centre.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I've already spoken about this, but I shall expand. Staff and professional support to the operations duty team consisting of the following, briefly: Collecting information about the combat deployment of the units of the 3rd Army; movements of the 3rd Army; movements of columns, and there were many of them, especially during the war; special events, the situation in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army; activities of the Siptar terrorist forces; and effects of NATO air-strikes and the activity of the NATO force in general, not only the air force. Also, it was very important to make sure that communications were operating round the clock, both vis-a-vis the operations centre of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia as well as towards all subordinate commands, which was done through the mediation table where there were encrypted and non-encrypted communications that were active, these communications functioned with smaller interruptions without any affect on the work of the operations team, I mean the interruptions didn't affect them, and they worked throughout the war. A very important component was the computer support to the -- to the centre and also electronic surveillance information. Radar images were particularly invaluable, they were obtained through a special unit that made it possible for the operations duty team to act on-line, in realtime, by correcting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could interrupt you. Mr. Aleksic, you've set out in the witness's statement a number of the aspects of the -- his responsibilities. Is this sort of detail that we are now getting an essential part of your case? If it is, we won't interrupt; but if it's unnecessary for us to know this, then there's little point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Thank you, Your Honour. I do understand. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Obradovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do move on, I just want to ask one question. In paragraph 3 of your statement, Mr. Obradovic, you tell us that during 1999 you became the head of the 3rd Army operations centre. And then you go on to say: "And further, until my retirement, I worked as an assistant to the commander of 3rd Army intelligence and morale department." Now, is that a separate job which you got later, after the war; or were you doing both jobs together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. During the war I was only chief of the operations centre. Towards the end of 1999, I became assistant commander of the army, not for intelligence but for information and moral guidance, morale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- That is to say the end of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you said that you received a great deal of information. Tell us from whom and how this information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The beginning of April 1999, when it was already certain that there would be changes in the combat disposition of the units and in the location of the command posts in the activity of the forward command teams of the command of the 3rd Army and the command of the Pristina Corps, the commander of the 3rd Army issued an order adjusting operations duty in a new day, in-depth, down the subordination line of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this order, the subordinate commands, those subordinated to the commander of the 3rd Army, submitted regular and extraordinary combat reports which, along with daily communications 24 hours a day, round the clock, between the leaders of the operations team and the commander units, provided a complete picture of the situation in the army units and the situation in the territory, which was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what the subordinate commands were, subordinated to the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: These were the following commands: The command of the Nis Corps, the command of the Pristina Corps, the command of the Nis Military District, command of the Pristina District, the 201st logistics base, the 202nd logistics base, the teaching centres of the 147th quartermaster's centre, the 186 technical, the 255th teaching centre in Kursumlija, then the 319th communications regiment, the 109th centre for electronic surveillance and monitoring. Then battalion rank units like the 3rd Battalion of the military police, the 3rd Motorised Battalion, the 559th auto-transport Battalion, the 19th institute for preventive medicine --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Fine, that will do. Could you just tell the Trial Chamber in what town the operations centre was, or rather, in the area of which town was the operations of the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the building of the command of the 3rd Army in the very centre of the town of Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: During the war were the headquarters of that centre changed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because one of my duties was to follow internet news, news agencies and all kinds of information that can be collected over the internet. About 20 days before the bombing of the building of the command of the 3rd Army there was a top list of certain targets, including the command of the 3rd Army. Subsequent assessment of this information led the commander of the 3rd Army and the Chief of Staff to change the location of the 3rd Army, and this was in the immediate vicinity of the command itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of April at 3.55 hours, two NATO aircraft struck the building with four rockets, the building of the command of the 3rd Army, destroying precisely the premises of the operations centre and the military court nearby. Due to this good assessment and the circumstances, we all survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of your previous answers you said, and you mentioned that in paragraph 18 of your statement as well, that you had information from the air-space on the basis of radar images and you could act in a timely fashion. Did the situation change during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This situation changed the very moment when Bulgaria opened its air-space and allowed NATO aeroplanes to fly over its territory, thus radically decreasing the time needed to act against the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 12th of April, 1999, the command of the Pristina Corps started from then on to send its combat reports to the operations centre of the 3rd Army and the operations centre of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to go back slightly about the attack on your operations centre on the 5th of April. On the 4th of April, was the whole command post moved from one place to another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operations centre is only one part of the command post. Other sectors of the command had already been relocated from the building. Only the operations centre was remaining there as an element of the operations staff sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it was the original building, the original command post, which was struck by the attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was -- had it been completely vacated before the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Presiding Judge, I have a picture if you want to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not necessary, thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just briefly, a few other matters. Are you aware that for the entire duration of the NATO aggression from end March to mid-June, was General Pavkovic ever present on the premises of the operations centre of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No. He authorised the Chief of Staff, General Stojmirovic, who occasionally visited us and gave us instructions, but on the day when the building was bombed he took care to find out whether everything was all right, whether everybody was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You as head of the operations centre, were you ever issued by General Pavkovic any order to leave out any information from combat reports or did he in any way influence the drafting of the combat reports and the information covered?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't, and he was practically unable to because combat reports were drawn up every day by new officers on duty. So he couldn't have talked that many people into that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Questions from any other Defence counsel? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. My name is Tomislav Visnjic; I represent General Ojdanic and I have a few questions for you. Can we just make one correction. In your statement, paragraph 2, you talk about the period when you were chef de cabinet of the 3rd Army commander and you list the commanders under which you served.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question is: When was General Vukovic commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think he became one in 1991 or 1992, because he was the one who actually brought me to the post of chef de cabinet of the 3rd Army command. He was then Chief of Staff. General Uzelac was the commander, but General Uzelac was already outgoing and General Vukovic was in the process of forming his team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That raises a question for me. First of all, that information is in paragraph 3 of our copy of the statement. You say it's in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking on B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it shouldn't matter. Presumably the paragraph numbers should be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the second question or the second matter that it raises is that Vukovic is not referred to in my paragraph. So, Mr. Aleksic, do we have the final version of the statement at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Vukovic is not listed in my text; that's the reason why I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may clarify, Your Honours. I did not mention General Simonovic either, I served under him, too, or General Perisic, I just listed a few names that--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. That's not helpful because they are mentioned in your statement even though they weren't mentioned today. You were only asked a few questions, nothing like the number in the information here. So are you saying the paragraph you're referring to is paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my version it's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Aleksic, why is there that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, the only mistake, the only discrepancy between the Serbian and the English text, was the paragraph 2. In B/C/S paragraph 2 includes all this information, part of it is only in para 3. That is something that must have occurred during translation. As for Mr. Vukovic, the witness had not mentioned him in the B/C/S version either; that's what he just explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean, though, that all the paragraph numbers thereafter are wrong? Where the B/C/S says paragraph 2 -- sorry, paragraph 3, we will have paragraph 4 in English, and so on. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we've just corrected that, but I will be able to tell you more in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to find the references.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, while you were chef de cabinet to the 3rd Army commander, any one of these commanders, what was the procedure like for drafting the actual orders as a formative document signed by the commander? Let's say that at one point the commander orders you to prepare a -- an order and you and chef de cabinet or somebody else takes up that task. You make a draft and then take it to the commander to the signed.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I would first have the -- have to say a few words about the methodology followed by General Samardzic, who was the last. His principle was the following: He would get an order from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, he would study it too with his assistants, the narrow circle of his command, including me; he would assign tasks and give deadlines. And they would each make their own draft with the accompanying documentation, such as maps and everything else that an order of that level has to include. And then he would give it to me to make radical cuts in it without sacrificing vital information, and I would do that with my assistant Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So once you have prepared this final version and submitted it to the commander of the 3rd Army, he would sign it and what is the procedure then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he is making an order on his own behalf, a "zapovest," a command of the 3rd Army command, he would again summon all his assistants and discuss it. But if it is just a proposal to the Supreme Defence Council or the Supreme Command, then I don't know what happens at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you what's going on in your office. You present a final draft of a document.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in my office, nothing happens. Nothing happens in my office except my personal work on those documents; everything else takes place in the office of the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who brings documents to him to be signed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you said that once these drafts with accompanying documentation had been prepared they would be given to you to make radical cuts without sacrificing vital information. What do you mean by "radical cuts"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only meant those cases when we were drafting a proposal by the 3rd Army commander to the Supreme Command Staff or wherever in Belgrade he was going. But when he was about to prepare an order on his own behalf as 3rd Army commander, then my job was very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you did not present the 3rd Army commander with any documents for signature?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After our usual preparatory work, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But when you were preparing a final version of a document, this abbreviated version as you described it, how many copies would you make?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I had one copy in my laptop and one copy for him, but let me clarify again. The document I prepared for him was practically his introduction on the basis of which he would make a report either to the Supreme Defence Council or the Supreme Command Staff, I don't know. Other documents remained intact. These forwards made by his various assistants for various sectors are the only thing that were -- was abbreviated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is important. Let's make a distinction. Did you have some sort of log-book into which you registered documents? So when you had a document signed by the commander, what happens to it technically but it needs to be logged in?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The document I prepared is practically his introduction to the combat documents that follow, and it is registered only informally, only within the office itself. When that paper is transformed into some sort of order, some sort of formal document, then it is entered into appropriate registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who verified the documents signed by the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, depending on which assistant had prepared it. The commander signed things within his own remit. Once the commander signs a document for the logistics assistant, the logistics assistant takes it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Where was the stamp?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The stamp of the army command was in a special office that held also the register and files. The command of the 3rd Army had its own stamp that said: "Command of the 3rd Army, office of the commander," and there were three numbers. Only special documents related directly to the commander were registered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness P1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's one of the combat reports of the 3rd Army, the exact date is 13 April 1999, it's in the package of documents that accompany your statement. Could you please look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, where did this document originate, I don't mean who wrote it, but I mean whose archives was it originate from?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by the number, I recognise this number of the register. It originated from and was filed with the files of the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the last page.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Supreme Command Staff, sector for operations and staff affairs?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that it comes from the archive that belonged to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Which means that it was prepared at the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the right, top corner, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what is written in Cyrillic: "Attachment number 1," on this document, that's not what you sent out from the 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not part of the format nor was it according to the rules on official correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at document P2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move off this -- I'm afraid I didn't understand that. "Attachment number 1" is written on it. Now, what's the point you're making, Mr. Visnjic, that the document was not sent or these words were not on it or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I wanted to get there slowly with the witness, but I don't think it's a problem for me to tell you straight-out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, you don't need to, but I may come back then to have it clarified later. Continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you see before you a document of the same date, this time it's a combat report from the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the last page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Last page we see the stamp and the date, it's the stamp of the Supreme Command Staff, which means this document, too, was received by the Supreme Command Staff on 13 April 1999; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, could you look at the first page again, right-hand top corner. We see attachment 1A. To the best of your knowledge, the command of the Pristina Corps did not write this kind of thing "attachment 1," "attachment 1A" either?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I am certain it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But we established with both documents that they were received at the Supreme Command Staff on the same date, and neither the 3rd Army command nor the Pristina Corps command had the habit of placing this indication in the right-hand top corner of such documents. Do you agree with me that it's possibly -- most probably the document was made at the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know such thing, and I had no access to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But it was not made in your command and it was not made in the Pristina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's up to you to draw a conclusion. I cannot tell you what happened on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: Are you aware that -- that the combat reports of the 3rd Army and the combat reports of the Pristina Corps were an integral part as attachments 1 and 1A of every report that the Supreme Command Staff compiled and sent up the chain to the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of personal communication with -- between Colonel Ivkovic -- with Colonel Ivkovic, I could reach that conclusion, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to draw your attention to P2005 and 4D10 -- P2005 also has the same marks on it. So perhaps conclusions can be drawn for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, you've helped me clarify some issues. Now I would like to go back to paragraph 19 of your statement in which you say -- well, it's actually paragraph 20 in English, and there you say that regular as well as interim combat reports of the 3rd Army command and the Pristina Corps command, intelligence and security information there were, of course, occasionally controlled by command and field units fully provided the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army with an objective and consistent control or insight into the 3rd Army Pristina Corps units, the situation at the state border, crucial events on the territory, especially connected to movements and protection of civilians, activities of terrorist groups, and so on?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say that they made it possible to have an objective and continuous insight into, in your system of values is that something that does not allow for any other possibility?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, philosophically you're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said this, did you inspect all the sources you mentioned here in paragraph 19, that is, intelligent and security well first let me ask you this: Did you look at all the intelligence information of the 3rd Army in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to be precise here. Combat reports were drawn up by designated officers in all the sectors of command within the duty operations team so that the intelligence man would write up the first paragraph of the combat report. The operations man would write up the second paragraph. The officer in charge of mobilisation and manpower levels would write the next. The logistics man or the rear man would write the next paragraph. As I was a member of the team and I worked -- I was on duty two plus one days, and then after my day of leave, of rest, I would come back and I would study all these items. And then the operative -- operations centre team had to write up a war diary, so that from this information one could gain an insight into the situation in the army, the events on the ground, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you're saying this on the basis of the daily and interim reports of the 3rd Army of the Pristina Corps, not on the basis of the intelligence and other reports?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the security organ sent that up his chain of command and this was confidential, it was kept secret from me; the same applies to the intelligence organ. They would simply give us the most important operation that -- information that had to do with the enemy, electronic activities, prediction of enemy activities, and so on and so forth. So for a man of average intelligence, that was quite sufficient to gain an objective picture of the situation in the army and the main tasks in the forthcoming period, in the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, we had three witnesses here who said that in their chain of reporting, not the one that went through you, some information failed to reach the staff of the main command, or rather, the Supreme Command Staff, and I'm referring especially to intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could not happen for the security officer not to write up item 5 of the daily report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say that based on these reports one could gain an objective and continuous insight into the situation, the activities on the ground, and especially movements of and protection of the civilian population, so when you say "movements of the civilian population," can you tell us in how many combat reports of the command of the 3rd Army which passed through your hands are movements of civilians, the civilian population, mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that, especially as a large part of the communication with the operations centres and the duty operations offices were by phone, by protected lines, so that this information was transmitted -- they were on security lines, so the information was transmitted when the situation required it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I were to tell you that this information was contained in only three combat reports of the 24th of March, the 10th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These movements of the situation and that information, do they have any -- is it significant to know who set the population in motion, that's important for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, I have a correction for the transcript. It should be 24th of March, 10th of May, and 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question hasn't been answered, though. The question was: Would you be surprised to be told that information about population movement was contained in only three combat reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be surprised because the Army of Yugoslavia, the 3rd Army, and the Pristina Corps did not have it within their competence to monitor movements of the population unless these interfered with the deployment of the troops or when the KLA was disrupting the shield, the protection. That's why this information isn't there. It's probably in the competent MUP organs because they were the civilian authorities and they dealt with protection of the civilian population. So that would be the logical answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This takes me back to this sentence in paragraph 20 in the English version which says: "Objective and continuous insight in connection with movements of the civilian population." So if I understood you precisely, you have now described precisely what sort of movements were reported here?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, are you aware that the commander, or rather, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command sent an order to all subordinate units, strategic groups, on the 29th of March, ordering that reports of the judicial organs be included in the combat reports?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that order, but by induction one can conclude that if an order is carried out in practice the subordinate commands report on it. And usually a report in its preamble says: Pursuant to such and such an order, I did this and that. So you could conclude that from those preambles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good morning.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Djuro Cepic; I appear for the defence of General Vladimir Lazarevic. I have only a few questions for you. I understood from your statement and from your testimony today that you spent the greatest part of the war in the city of Nis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did refugees from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in the war time-period arrive in the city of Nis?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: As the intensity of the NATO air-strikes grew, the intensity of the refugee columns grew also; there is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, that doesn't actually answer the question you were -- you posed. Do you not want an answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honour, with next couple of questions I will clarify everything what is relevant about that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, there's a very simple question, he should answer that first, about Nis, that is important. I mean, he hasn't answered that, it's just a vague reply, and I think he should first answer that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to clarify very, very specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, did any refugees from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija arrive in Nis during the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the reason for their arrival in Nis?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The only reason was fear of the bombing, fear for their nearest and dearest, and all nationalities arrived in Nis, mostly Serbs, Montenegrins, but also Albanians, Turks, and so on. The former had relatives in the city of Nis. They were saving the lives of their children first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should make it clear to you, Mr. Cepic, that I consider that answer valueless coming from this man without any foundation indicated for coming to that conclusion, no division at all of the proportions that he's talking about, and bearing in mind the sort of evidence we excluded from the Prosecution case taken by people like Human Rights Watch and so on. If you think that has achieved anything, then I should remove that thought from your mind. I'm actually surprised the question was not objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, I will continue in this way with next two questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in the city of Nis, apart from military targets, did bombs also fall on civilian buildings and were there any civilian victims?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Nis all the time and I was a witness to this round-the-clock bombing of civilian facilities, too, such as the market in Nis on a market day and there were no military facilities in the vicinity; the city hospital; the Duvaniste neighbourhood; and some other civilian centres within the city of Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: After these air-strikes and bombings of civilian facilities in Nis, did citizens of Nis leave the town for that reason?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in droves, especially women and children. Whoever had a weekend cottage somewhere or relatives elsewhere, they would leave Nis. Children interrupted their schooling, the university stopped operating. All the public utilities and services continued operating and the defence provided assistance in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before he begins just for the record and for your information, we had provided draft versions of witness statements to the parties for their own preparation purposes, but what was filed in e-court this morning is the final version and the paragraphs all match up word for word with each other. So there's no problem with the matching up of B/C/S and English paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem for me is knowing what I'm working with in the hard copy that you sent to us. Am I working with a draft?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can answer that. If your paragraph 2 contains the information that Mr. Visnjic was talking about this morning in the B/C/S then you've got the right one, but then you're probably not reading B/C/S anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This was submitted on the 19th, which was Friday, in the morning, 9.36 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there's been a modification since then, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before we leave that, Your Honour, it causes a problem for me, too, working from that hard copy and then finding out today that it's something different. We're supposed to get the statements 48 hours ahead of time, and I got the a supplemental information on another statement and that's easier to work with than to have the whole thing replaced. Now, if all that happened was that paragraphs 1 and 2 got combined into one paragraph in the B/C/S, then all I have to do is add one to each of the other numbers in English to follow along, but that's not what happened. I see in the B/C/S there are 29 paragraphs, there are only 28. As best I can figure out with my limited becoming is there's something happens around paragraph 20 of the B/C/S, and it appears there's something in B/C/S there that's not in the English somewhere between paragraph 20 and 23 of the B/C/S. But I don't know enough B/C/S to figure that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's no substantive change at all. I think it was just a matter of getting the paragraphs to match up with each other number-wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please bear in mind, Mr. Ackerman, that the need to give a final version to the parties 48 hours before the witness gives evidence, and I would certainly, for one, rather never have a draft at all. I'd rather have my copy immediately beforehand long enough to read it than ever to be assisted with a draft. I can understand why it might be of assistance to the parties themselves to have a draft but not for the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, sometimes the witnesses arrive in town and look at their statement once they get there and say, Oh, I didn't notice that before, that's a mistake. Now, we can file a supplemental, like the Prosecution did. I'm not sure that makes it easier, but we could do that if that's what's preferred, but that happened all the time during the Prosecution case the night before the witness would come on we would get that long supplemental statement so that wasn't provided 48 hours before either. So they have nothing to complain about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Hannis is suggesting that the mechanics of that are easier to work with than a completely rejigged statement. Now, even though there's minor rejigging, as you say, in this case, it probably looks a lot more than it is because of the change in numbers. So I hope you can between you work out an adequate way of working together, and I would rather spend time here listening to the evidence and hope that that can be resolved in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I have one more point that I want to -- I did get a supplemental information for the next witness with four changes and that's much easier to follow and incorporate. And I still don't -- haven't seen what's loaded in e-court for this witness, but in paragraph 23 of his B/C/S statement that I was provided on Friday, I see something here that I don't see in English or I guess it's -- I'm sorry, it's in paragraph 21 of the B/C/S. It appears to be a reference to some kind of bombs and rockets and radioactive something or rather, and I don't see that anywhere in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, or maybe, Mr. Aleksic, maybe you can deal with this. I leave it to you to sort out a method of working with Mr. Hannis that works to your mutual satisfaction, but on this particular point is this something added in paragraph 21 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my version is from September and nothing was added. In the Serbian version it's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The matter that's concerning you, Mr. Hannis, it's not what's in paragraph 19 of the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I -- I thought I found that. Paragraph 19 of the English I thought was paragraph 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to be finished your cross-examination by half past?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's go on and see if you can sort it out together at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, good morning. You told us that you became the chief of cabinet of the commander of the 3rd Army in 1992, and I understand you served under several different generals in that position. I have a question for you: During the time that you were chief of cabinet for General Perisic and later General Samardzic, what were your duties under those two generals?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just say the following: The function of chef de cabinet is a specific one. It does not have any strictly defined military or regulatory duties; it depended on the person of the commander. For example, General Perisic was an introvert who kept most information to himself. He kept it in his head. So he used his cabinet or office less than other commanders, he used it the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about under General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Samardzic relied on his cabinet to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you then told us that at the beginning of 1999, sometime in January, you were appointed chief of the operations centre of the 3rd Army command. Who took up your old job as chief of cabinet then, in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Savic took over who was a close collaborator of General Pavkovic in the Pristina Corps. He was the commander of the Pristina Military District to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall his first name?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Savic, Vojkan was either his name or his nickname, but that's the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your new job as chief of the operations centre, would that be viewed as a step up or a step down or a step sideways from your old job as chief of cabinet?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav national army and the Army of Serbia and Montenegro, I retained the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand you kept the same rank, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: As soon -- well, the Chief of the General Staff was one and then it went up to 20, a corporal or something at the level of the tactical group. So the number marked your position, your rank, your position in the military organization in a specific, particular military organization.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I'm afraid that in the record we don't have the necessary translation of the term the witness is using, it's the term "polozajna grupa," position group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One position in a command is defined by one's rank and by one's position group. As for the rank I had, I kept the rank of colonel and also the same position group when I was chief of the centre. So it is roughly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand about rank. I'm not clear about position group. Can you explain to me a little bit about what those are and give me some examples?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I will. Position group, it's basically your pay grade to put it in the simplest terms. You say if you're in group 10 you have 100 euro and then 190 if you belong to another group. I'm putting it in the simplest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In the operations centre, other than I guess before the war you would receive operations reports from the Pristina Corps; and after the war they're called combat reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No. Sometime in the spring of 1998 the commander of the army made a decision or an order came from the General Staff, I cannot say for sure, that reports should be called combat reports because basically there was a combat situation in a large part of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army. So combat report was the right word to use; however, a combat report meant a far broader quantity and quality of information, and that is what the commander decided to do or he received orders to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when in 1998 that came about, that there was a change that these reports should be called combat reports? You said in the spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the month of April or was it May, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 3rd Army at that time? Was that General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General Samardzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Perisic had already gone on to be Chief of Staff of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then in 1999, other than combat reports, were there other kinds of reports you received from the Pristina Corps; and if so, can you tell us about those?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I explained that a few moments ago. It's not only the operations centre, but also in the sectors of the command. There were sector reports that were received in terms of logistics, then security, morale, and so on. Abbreviated versions of these professional reports that are far more extensive found their own place within the combat report, too. For the operations duty team to be "au courrant" all the time in terms of the situation in the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally see those other kinds of reports or did you only see the summaries that were put into the combat report?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can just say the following: What happened very often was that that officer from the sector of logistics, for instance, would also be a member of the operations duty team. And then in that position he'd write both, so that was objectively my position and that is how I could see it, but otherwise no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In one of your answers to Mr. Aleksic at page 6, line 13, today you said: "The beginning of April 1999 when it was already certain that there would be changes in the combat disposition of the units and in the location of the command post in the activity of the forward command teams of the commander of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps ..." I have a question for you. How was it or why did it become certain that there were going to be changes in April 1999? What had happened or what was happening then that made it clear to you that there were going to be those kinds of changes?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't hard to tell. The chief of the Supreme Command Staff and the commands of armies and corps appraised the situation and realised what would happen, and they appraised this right. They knew that there would be a NATO aggression, an escalation of Siptar terrorism. Then the commander of the 3rd Army acted in a preventive fashion, combat disposition of the units, the best location of command posts, and in terms of protecting the units themselves, because the OSCE team actually played the role not of verifiers of events, but they were reporting on positions of command posts, deployment of units that could be seen from the report of the team for cooperation with the OSCE that I personally had occasion to see. So it wasn't difficult to assess what would happen. However, no one could envisage that it would be that cruel in terms of attacking civilian targets, civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that clear from the 23rd or 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was clear, I'm saying, but that's when the decision was made to start carrying this out. When the commanders actually made this assessment, I don't know for sure, but I personally made that kind of appraisal a lot earlier. Then there was a decision of the commander of the army that commanders of all the subordinate units, also in the beginning of April, prepare their decisions for protection or defence from aggression. I think that this happened sometime on the 5th of April, so they defined the locations where the army commander approved the decisions of each and every individual commander from the NATO aggression and the escalation of Siptar terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, wasn't the change that you're talking about or the changes that you're talking about in early April 1999 a result of the fact that the VJ, in coordination with the MUP, had accomplished a large part of an objective of removing KLA terrorists and a significant portion of the Kosovo Albanian civilian population; and now, in early April, they could start preparing to defend against an attack from NATO ground forces?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the Army of Yugoslavia had very serious and capable intelligence officers, and they knew what was going on. In the border area near Albania and in NATO bases and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in SFOR, and in other countries, and what was being prepared for the country of Yugoslavia, it was no problem to assess that and to react to that. If that could have been a step of deterrence, well the NATO command decided -- if the NATO command decided to sacrifice a group of Siptar terrorists so that this would be foreplay for a NATO land invasion -- well, we prevented that kind of developments from happening in advance. The Army of Yugoslavia -- well, that's why Mr. Visnjic said, there were only three reports that we mentioned -- where we mentioned the movements of the population. The army did not do that. The army, whenever possible, helped the civilian population, irrespective of ethnicity. Of course, I'm excluding some individual cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I taught you talked about part of your job being to monitor the international media, the internet and the media reports; that was part of what you did in the operations centre, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, yes. This was a duty outside the extent of -- well, it was a question of my level of education and training, and the commander believed that I could follow what was going on in the world and that we could get relevant political information in this way, in terms of assessing what the future developments might be in the course of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the course of doing that then you must certainly have been aware of at least the reports in the international media about hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanian civilians flowing out of Kosovo and into Macedonia and Albania in the first ten days or two weeks of the war. You saw those reports, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. But the first thing I saw and read was an analysis of the Cato [Realtime transcript read in error "cadre"] Institute for Washington where things were viewed in a far more realistic way, so this was my analysis of reference when I looked at the other reports that you are referring to that were highly tendentious. If you look at the dates involved, if you see the time-frame involved, you see that the major civilian population movements coincided with the NATO air-strikes. I saw the US senator when in Tirana he spoke to many refugees and they all said that they fled from NATO bombings --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment. Your Honour, I think the witness will confirm what he said, page 35, line 15, is the Cato Institute in Washington, not the cadre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I stopped you, Colonel, because you had answered my question and you were going on to something else. Apart from what you said you saw the US senator in Tirana spoke to many refugees and they all said. How do you know that all of them that the senator spoke to said they fled from NATO bombings? What was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say all senators, I said one senator, James Inhofe and there are many others, and these are agency reports. And there's Ms. Prentice, who was out in the field and who seriously Mr. Jamie Shea's reports and NATO reports and briefings. There were some people who had a far more realistic view of what was going on; however, there was no proof that this was done by the army according to some plan and intent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Richard Munz, who was a doctor, a physician in Stenkovac, he confirmed, for instance, that not a single woman had been raped out of the 60.000 who were examined --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not a question you were asked. You said there were people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, do you understand the system that operates here, that you answer questions? You don't come with a prepared agenda that you will expand upon. So please listen to the questions and answer them as they're address to you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that the operations centre in Nis was moved before it was struck by bombs. How many times did the operations centre change location during the war, just that one time or did you move a number of times?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Just that one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did you relocate to?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Very close to the command, only about 20 metres away. So at the moment of the bombing we were all black but we were all alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in what -- what sort of facility or building were you housed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was part of a complex where the military construction office was, the military library. So that's where it was, not exactly there but in the vicinity, in the sector within a 20- to 30-metre radius.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was the command located? You say 20 or 30 metres away. Was it in the same building or a different building?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's a block of buildings within that compound, so one building follows another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the nature of the buildings in that compound or the nature of that compound, was that a civilian housing compound or was it a school? What was it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The army command was the army command, next to it was the military court, and then these auxiliary military buildings if I can call them that. Nearby there were apartment buildings, absolutely; however, fortunately they didn't use bombs but they used rockets and they are far more precise. So the operations centre and the military court were targeted with surgical precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But only that first time and not again after the 12th or 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So they were only targeted that one time, not again after you moved?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They never discovered where we were again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that I think on the 12th of April, 1999, the command of the Pristina Corps started from then on to send its combat report, not only to you in the ops centre in the 3rd Army, but also to the ops centre in the Supreme Command. And tell us again why that was done?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I just know that that's the order that arrived, and I can only assume that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command had the idea of getting information far more quickly about what was going on in the zone of the Pristina Corps and in the 3rd Army so that from a command point of view he could act more efficiently, however, that is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that the Supreme Command may have had a concern that not all the information from the Pristina Corps was being completely and accurately forwarded from the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is technically impossible. Quite simply, I told you how many parallel information channels there were going on at the same time. You can see what was going on. It was virtually impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, we have to have a break just now. Today that will be at half an hour at this stage to allow the parties to sort out any difficulty about your statement. While that break's ongoing, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has the position of this statement been clarified, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Somewhat, Your Honour. There is a portion in the B/C/S that was not translated in English. I've been given that translation. The B/C/S that's in e-court now has 29 paragraphs; the English only has 27, and that's because I think what in English paragraph 20 in B/C/S it only goes to the colon in line 3 of our English paragraph 20. And then B/C/S paragraph 21 is what is paragraph A or sub-A in the English paragraph 20. And B/C/S 22 is what is sub-B with some additional language that talks about occasional delays in finding out about the crimes and carrying out on-site investigations, but it includes a rather provocative phrase about "as the war went on and NATO leaders were losing their composure and control we saw carpet bombing," et cetera, et.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one I have has 28 paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the English, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The English, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was the one you got on Friday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I'll get an up-to-date one later. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will -- we're filing a motion today to substitute exhibits in e-court so that the English and B/C/S statements will be the same and have the same language in them and everything. I apologise to the Court for this confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, Colonel, one of the things I'm having difficulty understanding is your -- your position was bombed once and then you moved into military buildings. Didn't you have concern that you would be bombed again in that new location?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a classical type of military building, it's one of the facilities, one of the logistical facilities of the army. And we didn't have much choice anyway because some of the communication lines related to electronic support forced us to be so close by. But we camouflaged ourselves tactically and technically, so it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say it was not a classical type of military building. Before the war, what was it used for?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, the military construction directorate is an institution that employees civilians, who built and do interior decoration of facilities, the military library is not typical military institution, so it's not a directly military purpose they serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned that when the -- when that bombing occurred at -- a part of the operations centre's documents were destroyed. Can you tell us which documents, which kinds of documents were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The operations centre has for a long time preserved its documents and batches of files that were both registered and not registered. We had enough time to take only those that were operationally the most necessary, papers that were reflected in other documents of the 3rd Army command, so that didn't really matter. I'm sorry that some of my personal document has burnt, but what can we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you took your most immediately important documents with you when you moved prior to the bombing, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a little bit about the operations centre and how you worked, and I think it was a question from Mr. Visnjic. You said that General Pavkovic never gave you any order to leave any information out of combat reports. You said he was practically unable to because combat reports were drawn up every day by new officers on duty, so he couldn't have talked that many people into that kind of thing. How many shifts worked at the operations centre? Did you have three eight-hour shifts per day or two 12-hour shifts or how was that done?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: One team was on duty for 12 hours, with the proviso that I as head of the centre and two of my associates worked 48 hours in a go with 12 hours of rest -- sorry, 24 hours of rest. So the responsibility lay with the chief of the operations team, the possibility for an army commander to do the kind of thing you are suggesting is absolutely non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the suggestion originally came from Mr. Visnjic, but let me ask you, you say in paragraph 4 of the English and paragraph 3 of the B/C/S in your statement that the operations team on duty consisted of three officers ranked as lieutenant-colonel or colonel. You were one. Who were the other two by name?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think you're a bit confused. You have to distinguish between the establishment composition of the operations centre and the operations duty team, that included me and one lieutenant-colonel, who later became a colonel, and a third one, so one colonel and two lieutenant-colonels. That was the establishment element. The operations duty team was a non-establishment component that was formed by the commander for the following week, let's say, and those people had their establishment positions in various sectors of the command. They were on duty only for those 24 hours; after that, they were free, and that included the leader of the team. As the combat situation changed and as people left for the forward command post of the 3rd Army command, the teams were on duty more and more often; the frequency of their shifts increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I'm confused --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I'm confused, and perhaps I am, but your statement says: "The continuity of work was provided throughout the shift work of ODT," which appears in your statement to be the abbreviation for operations team on duty. "The team consisted of three officers ranked as lieutenant-colonel and/or colonel." So is your statement incorrect?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I don't think you understand me. You have to distinguish between the operations centre and its personnel and the operation team on duty. The operation team had seven or eight officers from all the various sectors of the command that were on duty that particular day and they were free the next day, whereas people from the operations centre created the necessary technical and logistical support as employed there. That's the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the kind of work that you were doing and the people that were under you were doing was work that was done around-the-clock, 24 hours a day during the war, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to understand how that coverage was made. You said before that I think you were on for 48 hours with -- and then had 24 hours rest. Say this is Monday morning, what time did you go to work and what time did you leave?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you worked 48 hours straight?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Without --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Without sleep. Occasionally when there was bombing going on, without sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But sometimes you would sleep part of that 48 hours when you were on duty if there was no bombing?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I found it difficult to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you would have 24 hours off?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand. And the 24 hours you were off, who was working in your position, another colonel, another lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The two that were left. One of them continued to work for the next 48 hours, and that's how it rotated continuously. Always one of us from the operations centre was on the team, the team on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were the names of those two others?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: One was Lieutenant-Colonel Gligorijevic, I forget his first name; and the other one was Lieutenant-Colonel Caslav Zivkovic. The name eludes me for the moment for Gligorijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time you were off and they were on duty, you don't have personal knowledge of any conversations they might have had with General Pavkovic, for example?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I don't, but when I come back the next day he would inform me of what had happened in my absence of combat reports, anything peculiar in them, the specific combat tasks; and neither of these two collaborators ever told me anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in answer to a question from Mr. Cepic about citizens leaving Nis during bombing there. Did -- if you know, did those people just leave the town or did they actually leave Serbia? They didn't go outside the country of Serbia, did they? They just left the town of Nis to more remote areas?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was some young people unfortunately who left Serbia altogether, but the greatest part of the population ran away into the provinces, into the countryside, to their weekend cottages to pull out their families and children and even the personnel of the Pristina Corps [as interpreted] with the approval of the commander did the same so that the officers and soldiers wouldn't at least have to worry about their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, with your leave, just one correction in transcript, page 45, line 9 -- actually line 8, I think that the witness said "army," not the Pristina Corps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you mentioned people leaving and going into the countryside to their weekend cottages to pull out their families and children. And you went on to say: "Even the personnel of ... With the approval of the commander did the same." Personnel of which body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The officers of the army command who were detached seconded to the Pristina Corps or the forward command post. It was not looked upon unkindly if one tried to get one's family away from all this; it was quite human.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, we saw a few exhibits that were listed with your statement. When we got notice of what you were going to testify about, we were provided with a list of some exhibits that might be shown to you. During your time in the operations centre at the beginning of the war, were you receiving daily combat reports from the Pristina Corps every day, from the 24th and 25th of March on?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I received them every day, but they were not daily, they were combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. By "daily," I meant in the generic sense that every day you were receiving a combat report from Pristina Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There wasn't a day when you did not receive a report, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
