utterances.text: Only occasionally during intensive combat reports from various centres in Kosovo would be late, but then the methodology of work was the following. In order to -- for our report from the army command to be received in time by the General Staff, we would additionally later provide those elements that should have been in our report but were not because the relevant subordinate reports were late. So there was just a time delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your time as chief of cabinet under General Samardzic, were you aware of any occasions where General Samardzic had a problem with his then-subordinate General Pavkovic and what was being done with the Pristina Corps in Kosovo? Did you ever see any documents about that or hear any discussion about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Their conflict about the documents or their conversation? What are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any documents or hear any conversation about problems that General Samardzic was having with how General Pavkovic was using the Pristina Corps? Did you ever recall hearing anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in July I was present at a meeting of the Joint Command where General Samardzic attended and I attended, and I looked at the methodology of work. And at the end General Pavkovic got an assignment to prepare a proposal and General Samardzic had a problem with it, but it was later resolved ultimately through a joint proposal for the use of forces to break-up Siptar terrorists and other actions. So that disagreement was more of a constructive nature in the process of making a decision, but once the decision was made there was more discussion. The commander made his decision and it was implemented. Information was entered into the war diary on a daily basis, so you can see from it who decided what, on what day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the beginning of that answer you said "July." I take it that was July 1998, this meeting with the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, end July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that meeting took place and who else was there besides you, Pavkovic, and Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a group of civilians, officials, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic I believe was chairing, there was a representative from the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP. Mr. Minic opened the meeting, and the representative of the MUP was the first to come up with his evaluation of the situation, what he intends to do, then the operations man from the Pristina Corps presented what the army was going to do, and I believe specifically they reviewed a proposal related to a place called Junik and what to do there. And then Mr. Minic asked at the end, Do you have any requests? And you remember then Mr. Pavkovic insisted on special equipment, Kevlar vests, because it was a time when Siptar terrorists started massively using snipers. And then a proposal was made by the army commander. It was approved, later signed. That was the methodology I was able to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. After that July 1998 meeting, were you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, page 48, line 11, the witness said: That is approved by the army commander. The record says: It was approved. It should read: It was approved by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters repeat their request for the witness to speak a little less fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you want to take that up and have it clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear what Mr. Petrovic said. Was that your answer, that it was approved army commander?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention any Petrovic -- you mean him? Oh, no, I'm sorry, I meant I didn't refer to any Petrovic in the context of the meeting. I'd forgotten the counsel's name, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But part of your answer was you said: "And then a proposal was made by the army commander, it was approved, later signed." Which army -- well, first of all, are you saying the army commander approved the proposal?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, judging by what you're saying, it seems the army commander approved his own proposal. No, the operations man from the Pristina Corps, then under General Pavkovic, suggested what to do; then the army commander reviewed it in his office, inserted his objections and comments; it was returned for additional processing. Later on an order was written on that basis, and that's how it was done. Those meetings were attended by a team of operations men from the Pristina Corps on the orders of the army command, and of course the commander of the Pristina Corps. I happened to be there just by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need to follow-up on that a little bit. You said the operations man from the Pristina Corps suggested what to be -- suggested what to do. And then the army commander reviewed it in his office. You mean General Samardzic reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He reviewed it -- the commander of the Pristina Corps brought that proposal, showed it to the army commander, the army commander said or didn't say, because I wasn't there, what he thought. The writing of the order followed shortly, and that's the course things followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then army commander, General Samardzic, looked at it, maybe suggested some changes, and then sent it back to General Pavkovic, the head of the Pristina Corps, who then wrote an order of how things were to be done?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The combat use of units was signed by the army commander because by then he was already at the forward command post and he stayed there until the end of the year. So it's a separate order, where the army commander had earlier ordered that he's the only one to approve the combat use of units. That was the logic of things and it was not disrupted. That can be seen from the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What time-period are we talking about then? Are we talking about 1998, while General Samardzic is still the army commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Petrovic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but page 50, lines, let's say, 8 and 9, he said: The use of units in keeping with, he said, Supreme Command Staff, and that's what's missing from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to follow that up, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, did you hear what the lawyer, Mr. Petrovic, said then and is that an accurate reflection of what you had said in your answer?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought we were talking about 1998, and as I understood it the Supreme Command Staff --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. As I understood it from other evidence, the Supreme Command Staff did not come into existence until the state of war was declared, and prior to that it was referred to as the General Staff, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: You're right. You're right. It's a slip of a linguistic nature. Of course what stuck in my mind that throughout the war it was the Supreme Command Staff, but at that time of course it was the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in that earlier answer when you said that there was a separate order where the army commander had earlier ordered that he's the only one to approve the combat use of units, were you referring to Samardzic as the commander of the 3rd Army or were you referring to General Perisic as the Chief of the General Staff or both?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Without knowing any details, I know the logic of things. I know for a fact that General Samardzic, the commander of the 3rd Army, ordered the effective use of units of the Pristina Corps; but it's certain that he got that order from the Chief of General Staff because it can't be otherwise. But I don't know the details, nor did I see the order of the General Staff prescribing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But were you aware that such an order had been issued by General Perisic, as Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware that he issued such an order, but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you mentioned that the operations centre had moved I think on the -- did you move on the 4th of April then, the day before it was bombed?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The last man and the last piece of equipment left on the 4th of April. We started taking things out a few days earlier, and some people had already moved to the new location, but the last person and I myself, we left on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that partly answers my question, because it seemed from the very first hours or first days of the war that NATO was targeting in large part command and control facilities of the VJ army. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I guess I had wondered why you hadn't moved sooner, but it sounded like you were starting to move a few days before the bombing actually occurred, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to your operations centre, was there a -- was there a war diary you kept in the operations centre or some sort of daily log?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The people from the operations centre and I myself in particular was tasked with keeping a war diary and I'm sure it's still in existence, I don't know where, but there must still -- it must still be there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my question if you knew what happened to it. Where would it have gone after the war? Do you know who would have been responsible for archiving it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to point out that the answer to Mr. Hannis's line 11 question does not appear in the transcript. It just goes to his next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the answer? What was the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't hear it, Your Honour. I didn't hear an answer. I don't know that there was one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the witness did not say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I saw him shaking his head yes and perhaps didn't hear an audible answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's of any real significance, Mr. Hannis. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to ask you about a couple of documents. Exhibit P2005, and I've got a -- I think I've got a hard copy here that I can have the usher hand you which might make it quicker.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In my English this is apparently a combat report from the 3rd Army command to the Yugoslav Army General Staff on the 27th of April covering the period for the 24 hours from 1800 hours on 26 April. Is this the kind of document that you would help prepare? I know if you go on the last page the authorisation for sending this telegram is from Colonel Kitanovic but my question is: Did you have any part in preparing this kind of report?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've practically answered that question already, but I'll repeat. My role and the role of the people in the operations centre was to create the best possible conditions for the operations duty team to do its work well, and that meant drawing up a good-quality report, providing good information technology support, bringing all the combat reports of the subordinate commands to the desk, and respecting the methodology of work established by the leader of the operations duty team. However, the people from the operations centre did not participate in compiling the combat report and neither did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see these reports when they went out or at any time?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, certainly. I saw them all because my task was to keep a war diary, and this forced me to look at all of them. And as far as I could, the reports coming from the subordinate units, although there was a large volume of paper coming in every day. But all the most important details had to be entered into the war diary, and this forced me to make an effort and look at all the most important information. And even when I was off on the next day when I came back, I would catch up and review as much as I could of those reports in order to register the events in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about the numbering of these documents on the first page at the very top left of my English there's a four-digit number 3821. Do you have any idea what that number refers to? In my English it appears right above "3rd Army command." Is there a perhaps a handwritten number on there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. These numbers have nothing to do with the reports. It's something that was done at a later date. I'm not aware of this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about the number under "3rd Army command, strictly confidential number 26-115," can you tell us -- can you tell us about that? What does 26 refer to?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That's the number in the log-book where documents were entered. The number of the log-book which existed in the operations centre in which the document would be entered under a certain number, 26, 100 through 116 or 117, 118, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you didn't see any other information, if you didn't see the word "3rd Army command," would you be able to recognise by that number, 26, that this document related to the 3rd Army command? Is there anything unique about that number? I'll need an answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I know 26 just as I know 92 or 455. These are numbers you see so often on those documents that they stick in your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we understand from other evidence in this case that 455 referred to the Pristina Corps in 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Pristina Corps, one of the sectors of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But sometimes we've seen other types of documents with a different number that appears to refer to the 3rd Army as well. Are those numbers -- is there more than one unique number referring to the 3rd Army depending on a topic or what part of the 3rd Army command it is? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you've just said, it was the part of the 3rd Army drawing up that document. Every sector and command of the 3rd Army had its own number, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; and they all had their log-books and the sub-numbers would refer to the topic, 115, 114, 116, that would refer to the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I had understood that 26 might refer to a particular unit and perhaps a particular subject matter with regard to that unit, and then the following number after the dash was chronological number or sequential number. So 26-115 would be the 115th document in 1999 referring to whatever 26 was, 3rd Army command or operations, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: And entered -- yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on this report, I'm not sure where to direct you to, it's under 2.1, activities, consequences, et cetera, it looks like about the ninth paragraph down, it's a small paragraph about awards or medals being handed out to members of the Pristina Corps. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: All I recall is the event from the report. I wasn't there. I didn't see it. I only know about it from the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to the -- I think it's on the last page B/C/S for you, it's under item number 8, corps activities for the next day. Do you see that item?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And about halfway down there's one that reads in the English: "Reception of part of the 72nd," I think it's an abbreviation for special brigade, "for joint planning and command of the forces engaged in Kosovo and Metohija." Do you see that one?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the 72nd Special Brigade, that was what, a special brigade?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Very special, very able, were operational, the pride of the Army of Yugoslavia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that at least a part of the special brigade came to Kosovo on or about that day? Do you know what that was about?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't appear in the reports, but it says here reception of part of the command, command, not unit. That's a big difference. As they were specialists for, among other things, anti-terrorist activities, somebody must have reached the assessment that they were needed in order to reach more efficient decisions for the destruction of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read the version you have there so I can see if my English translation matches what the translators say it says.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Reception of part of the command of the 72nd Special Brigade for unified command and control of the forces engaged in Kosovo and Metohija for joint planning and command in the forces engaged in Kosovo and Metohija." So it's quite clear, they came to assist in planning and commanding more efficiently. That was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly was part of the command of the special brigade going to make joint plans with General Pavkovic on how forces were going to be engaged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably General Pavkovic knows what they did. I wasn't there. But it says: "Reception of part of the command for joint planning and command," that leads to the conclusion that they had arrived to help with the planning and command. I don't know anything more about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Give me one moment, Colonel, and I'll see if I have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Hannis. Mr. Aleksic -- sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, my name is Toma Fila --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the matter you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the Joint Command, Your Honour. We've been talking about that for two years, so when I start introducing myself, I wonder whether my name is Toma Joint Command, but in any case it was not mentioned in the examination-in-chief, but it was mentioned in the cross-examination. So it remains hanging in the air, that's why I would like to clarify some points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The state of the information on it has greatly changed in these two years, Mr. Fila, but please continue if that's the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm asking. It would be boring otherwise, if it didn't change, I mean. Further cross-examination by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned that you happened to be with General Samardzic at a meeting of the Joint Command. I would like to know this: The chief of the staff of the 3rd Army was General Simic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are speaking Serbian so everyone understands us, but we need to make a pause between question and answer for the interpreters. Mr. Simic testified here, that's pages 15531 and 15532, and he spoke about the Joint Command, and he said more or less the following: That every evening around 1830 the corps commander of the Pristina Corps, General Pavkovic, would come to his office for him to issue -- for him, Samardzic, to issue orders to him. Then he went to a meeting of a body of some sort of coordinating body, colloquially known as the Joint Command. He would come back from there. If he had heard any suggestions from the MUP and if this was accepted by General Simic, who was acting on behalf of General Samardzic, evidently, then General Simic would issue an order. And then he would say: My order is law. Is that how things functioned in the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that General Simic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I gave you an example when I was at that meeting, but as to the chef de cabinet, every morning in the command of the army in Nis regular briefings were held of the narrow circle of the command, the commanding officers who were there. And then these issues were considered, cooperation or noncooperation with the MUP and so on. So I listened about this on a daily basis and I was a witness when the Junik issue was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your answer, you see, you -- well, in the question it was put to you that this coordinating body was colloquially known as the Joint Command. What does that mean? You seem to have agreed with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer indirectly, but I'm sure everybody will understand. I wrote up that war diary almost on my own using a large number of combat reports, other reports, orders, personal communication with the commanders, with the operations centres, and I can assert that in that war diary where the major decisions and activities of the 3rd Army, the 3rd Army area, the Pristina Corps are recorded, not in one single instance is the term "Joint Command" recorded. Furthermore in item 6 of every combat report there is an item called command and communications, if that command had been a serious command in a combat report in item 6, that change would have been recorded, that it had entered the chain of command of the 3rd Army, but that never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can you help me more specifically, what do you mean by accepting it was colloquially known as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't provide that name, but from that meeting I attended I would never term that body a command. It was a group of a people who listened to the assessments of the offices of the police, the offices of the army, heard their requests, issued no orders, and then if that's how it went and then from these papers, from these briefings, at the level of the collegium of the 3rd Army command, I never heard otherwise, so that conclusion follows from all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you -- just a second. Does "colloquially known as the Joint Command" mean that that's how you described it among yourselves, you talked about the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or never they even laughed at it, somebody made it up, somebody invented it and it turned up in the terminology but in the military practice and in the system command, it never turned up except for reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't go back over telling me it wasn't a formal organization in the command structure. Just try and deal with the question. You seem very defensive about the references to the Joint Command. We're just trying to get information about it. Now, how did -- did you talk about it with your colleagues as the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We did call it the Joint Command but in a pejorative sense. That was a term that existed, and we admitted existed, I admitted existed. But in view of its effects as regards commanding the army units, it acquired a pejorative meaning over time, and that's why it never appears in a single combat report of the 3rd Army or in the war diary of the 3rd Army, which I was in charge of. I would have entered it had it been important, because for every day in the war diary it says the commander of the army decided, the Chief of Staff decided or ordered, and the team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, there is no need to be so defensive about all this and go on forever answering a question I haven't asked you. Please just confine yourself to the question that you're being asked. It's as if you -- someone might suspect you have something to defend yourself against and no one's making any accusation against you. We just want to be clear about the facts. Now, it was you that mentioned the Joint Command in today's evidence, no one prompted you, you raised it. So I'm trying to be clear about what it is you were talking about when you raised it. What was the Joint Command that you were referring to in your evidence when you mentioned it today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Joint Command, as far as I was able to see from the documents I reviewed, was a group of civilians who had arrived to ensure better cooperation between the commands of the army and the command or the staff of the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija. That cooperation was generally good, but occasionally it was not. So their role was to make sure that that cooperation was better, but when something is referred to as a command and they do not have the competency or the infrastructure necessary to command, then it acquires a pejorative meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it was called that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think it was a good idea to coordinate the activity of the MUP and the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why give the body that was doing that a pejorative name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was a mistake made by someone, I don't know why, but in the mouths of the Army of Yugoslavia it's quite clear who the command is and what its powers are. I don't know where that name came from, but it suddenly surfaced and it's true that it was called the Joint Command, but that was just an ephemeral part of the whole story. The gist of it was that they did not have effective command powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me then just put a thought to you, no more than that, for your comment if you can assist us. Did the army perhaps think that the Joint Command was trying to interfere in the command structure, and therefore tried to ridicule its name or its composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't the intention of the army to ridicule it, but whoever named it named it wrongly, erroneously, and those people never even tried to issue commands in an effective command sense. I have seen documents which says "Joint Command" in the heading, but the log-book number is that of the Pristina Corps. The signature at the end of the document would be the signature of a commander of the Pristina Corps or the commander of the Pristina Corps. It's the practice in the army when an order is issued that the subordinate phones whoever issued the order and he would say, for example, Item 5.2 is not clear to me. But there is no infrastructure, no log-book, no staffing personnel infrastructure that would indicate that this was a real military command or a command -- any sort of command, so it never entered the army system of command, and as far as I've heard not of the MUP either. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm asking you about 1998. I'll ask you about that meeting, but do you know for how long this went on, these meetings in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that General Samardzic was in a hurry, so we entered the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. I'm not asking about the length of the meeting, but for how many months?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, from end July to end October 1998, that's when these meetings were held. I didn't hear about them anymore in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So may we conclude that you have information that these meetings attended by civilians also went on until October 1998, and after that you no longer heard of any meetings attended by civilians?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at that meeting with General Samardzic to see what was really going on there, you saw that the meeting was opened by Mr. Minic. What was his position at the time as a politician?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was in the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. He was Speaker of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the Federal Assembly, that's right, I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said there was several civilians there, you mentioned Nikola Sainovic. Can you tell us, at that meeting where the topic of discussion was Junik as far as I can recall, what did Nikola Sainovic do there? What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Sitting and listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Throughout the meeting did he issue an order to someone?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't even try.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Neither did Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the testimonies of numerous witnesses, including Minic and some others, it was said that that was a coordinating body where they went to hear the opinions of the army and the MUP about what was going on and that Sainovic was a representative of the federal government or cabinet who used that information in his conversations with international verifiers and others. Would you accept that opinion as correct based on what you saw and heard concerning these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as he didn't interfere in command, that's the only logical conclusion one can draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. That would be all I had to ask you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obradovic, you said earlier that as far as you were able to see from the documents you reviewed that the Joint Command was a group of civilians who had arrived to ensure better cooperation between the MUP and the VJ. Now, is that the position; and if it is, was Mr. Sainovic in a different position from the other civilians there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes, and then it was Mr. Minic who practically made a brief introduction and gave the floor to the officers of the MUP and the military officers. So I didn't know who was in this nomenclature, who was what in this group of civilians, and they weren't in uniform either. I don't even know if they have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to work out who it was that did the coordinating if all that Mr. Sainovic did was listen so that he could pass information on to other people. Who was it that -- among the civilians that was trying to coordinate the MUP and the VJ, as you described their function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment when I was there, Mr. Minic. After that, I wasn't interested, so I can't really answer that question of yours. And this kind of information did not appear in any report, that someone within this Joint Command from amongst the civilians ordered this or that, coordinated whatever. I cannot really answer. As for that particular day, it was Mr. Minic who was the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, I only ask you because it was you that said that it was a group of civilians who had arrived to ensure better cooperation. However, we can move on. Mr. Visnjic, what is it you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I wish to raise is something that pertains to part of the witness's statement, page 31 of the transcript, lines 8 to 25, where the witness says that in the spring of 1998 reports of the 3rd Army that were sent out got the prefix of combat, they were called combat reports, and that is the first time this was referred to, during Mr. Hannis's cross-examination. In relation to that, I have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please continue. It will probably take longer for you to explain than to do it. We have to try and avoid this constant to-ing and fro-ing across the courtroom. There's got to be more discipline in cross-examination, and hopefully you will raise additional cross-examination only when it's really necessary, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, could you please assist me with something. You said that sometime in the spring roughly, I see it says April or May, reports of the 3rd Army that were sent to the General Staff got the prefix combat, they were called combat reports; am I right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you please look at P923 now, page 15 English text and page 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will give you a reference straight away why I'm asking the witness about this. It has to do with the second part of the expert report of General Radinovic, paragraph 19, footnote 131. This was discussed in the transcript of the 18th of October, 2007, pages 17200 and then further on for the next 20 pages or so. So it is P923 in the B/C/S -- no, sorry, in English it's fine, 15, and in B/C/S it's 16, please. Now, Your Honour, on page 15 there is only the name of General Ojdanic, I'm talking about the B/C/S version. And then his remarks begin on page 16. It's very clear in English. Could we please have the top of the B/C/S version again. Thanks. Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I have to ask you something now, and I need this for the translation. Can you just read out to me the first paragraph that you see up here on page 15 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I understand you that this is General Ojdanic who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, could you please read it for me.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: "I request that as your deputy I receive combat reports of the commander of the 3rd Army and I suggest that this same report be received by the assistant for land forces and the chief of the first administration. Now I would like to give a suggestion and a proposal, General."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think you see that there is a difference between the B/C/S version and the English translation that we have here, that is one thing that I wanted to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we went over this in detail in the evidence of Radinovic. This is not an appropriate use of further cross-examination. Unless you've something else to deal with, please sit down and we'll move on. This is something you could perfectly easily have explained without any further questions of this witness. The evidence is there to be analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have to tell you one thing that this is the first time that we've heard information, that reports that the 3rd Army sent in 1998 were combat reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It all fits together like a jig-saw in the end, Mr. Visnjic. That's not an appropriate use of the privilege of further cross-examination. Please move on to something else if there is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of some of the Court's questions and the most recent questions of Mr. Fila, I have one document or two documents that I would like to show the witness, or I can direct the Court's attention to it and you can decide whether we need to address any questions to him or just rely on the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell me what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One is P1459, which is the 25 May report to the Supreme Command from General Pavkovic about non-subordination of the MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, if the point you're trying to make, Mr. Hannis, is that albeit this witness can only speak of things happening up until October but there is clear evidence of the Joint Command being referred to thereafter, then that's -- that doesn't need any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one of it relates specifically to his answer at page 60, line 11: "I wrote up that war diary almost on my own using a large number of combat reports, other reports, orders, et cetera; and I can assert in the war diary where the major decisions in the 3rd Army, Pristina Corps recorded in not one single is the term Joint Command recorded. I have Exhibit 2017 which is a combat report 3rd Army command on the 29th of April to the General Staff or Supreme Command Staff where there is a reference to a decision on the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. I think you should refer to that. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just asking you one thing. When it is taken that I said something, you can see full well that I asked the witness about 1998. From my questions there can be nothing that would lead us to 1999. If Mr. Hannis wants something, let him want it; if you allow him to do that, you have the right to do that, but not through me. He could have asked about 1999 himself when he had his time. The witness himself spontaneously, as you said, referred to Joint Command. I said please read 1998. I did not even mention 1999. That is why I'm opposed to having Mr. Hannis allowed to ask questions through me. He can do whatever he wants through you and whatever you allow him to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the result of your intervention and the way in which you conducted it has been that the witness has made various assertions about the period after October 1998, and that having happened it's clearly an issue that may be further explored. It's for us to decide whether to exercise our discretion to allow him to do so. Now, we will consult on that and I will let you know the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This undoubtedly arose from the examination by Mr. Fila, and therefore you are entitled to pursue that matter now in our opinion, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I just want to hand you a document, this is Exhibit P2017. It appears to be a 3rd Army command combat report dated 29 April 1999 addressed to the Yugoslav Army General Staff. And I think I've highlighted the portion near the bottom of page 1 that I'd like you to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the English for Your Honours and other English speakers it's on page 2 and it's the fifth paragraph up from the bottom, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read that out for us, Colonel, and we'll see if the translation matches what we have in English.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Measures were taken for the following regions to be blocked and tasks resolved in the spirit of the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There has to be an end to this, and we have allowed your opportunity, we've allowed Mr. Hannis that very limited question, and that's the end of the matter with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, it might be best to take the break at this stage so that we don't interrupt your next witness shortly into his evidence. So we'll break now and resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for putting -- but I'm putting this question when there's no one else here. It really is the wrong order of things when I ask after the cross-examination. I agree with you on that. However, the Joint Command is not referred to at all when witnesses are announced and there is nothing in the material there, so I cannot put any questions on the basis of what I receive beforehand. I do apologise for asking, but I only ask if the words "Joint Command" are uttered. If they are uttered during the examination-in-chief, I will deal with it when I'm supposed to, but if you have a better solution I'm prepared to go along of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have no problem with that and one of our earlier discussions earlier this morning was just to confirm that my decision to allow you to ask these questions earlier was the right one. Our only criticism is of the way in which you put the questions. It is cross-examination, and therefore you're entitled to put leading questions. But the more leading the nature of the question, the less valuable can be the answer. And you may assist yourself further by the way in which you approach the witness, although I understand why for reasons of time you've -- you do do it the way you have done so far. But you can go back and forward forever in proceedings of this nature. The line has to be drawn somewhere, but where the first mention of Joint Command is in cross-examination by Mr. Hannis, then if you have an issue to raise, generally speaking, we'll allow you to raise it. So we'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is General Mirko Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He will testify with a 92 ter statement and a little bit of live testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. Would you be so kind as to give us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, on 29th September this year, did you give a statement to the Defence team of Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read that statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The same, I would not change a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is 4D500. May I tender this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, General, but very briefly, about your military career, which positions you held in the 1990s, let us say, beginning with 1994.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Beginning with 1994, that is, 1st April 1994 I was assistant commander for information and morale in the 3rd -- in the Pristina Corps. I stayed in that position until 9 September 1997, when I reported to another duty in the 3rd Army command. In December 1997 I became assistant commander of the 3rd Army for information and morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you continued in that position throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, we have your statement which is an exhibit now and we are not going to go through all the paragraphs, but I would like your assistance on a couple of matters. In paragraph 12 of your statement you speak about the recording of an audio-cassette with a proclamation to the civilian population, warning them not to approach or enter military installations. Could you tell the Trial Chamber why that recording was made?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was made for preventive purposes, because between 120 and 130 military installations were in a way under observation and surveillance by Albanian separatists. That audiotape was made in Radio Pristina in end December 1998 in the Albanian and Serbian languages. The Albanian tape was made as a translation of the Serbian version, and the translation was done by the intelligence officer -- by one of the intelligence officers of the Pristina Corps, a native of that region who had perfect Albanian. And that was a succinct warning not to approach a military installation, lest force be used against any person who tries it. And a number of these cassettes were distributed to various installations and units so that they could use them to distribute the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your position as assistant commander for information and morale, did you go to lower-ranking units to expect and tour?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of my duties was to accompany the commander, but even without him I would tour and inspect fully or in part various installations. On the orders and without the orders of my commander, General Pavkovic, I toured and inspected various lower-ranking units of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And when you went to tour the units, what did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I talked with those units, I had briefings with lower-ranking units, and all those lower-ranking units attended by the commander of the army. His assistants usually held briefings. They would inform subordinates about the situation -- about -- the situation in the country and in the world, developments that are pertinent to the defence of the country, the steps taken by the General Staff to build up the defences of the country, with a focus on the units that we were touring.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I believe you answered you went on these tours even before the war began, before the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: During those tours, did you inform troops on preventive orders issued by the command of the 3rd Army and later by the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I made a special emphasis when touring the Pristina Corps combat groups and the attached units to draw the troops' attention to the things that General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic stressed, namely, that troops should be made specially aware of the need to observe and honour the rules and regulations of international humanitarian law. General Pavkovic's motto was humanity and then responsibility. General Lazarevic, his subordinates, said humanitarian principles are something that I place above the principle of military efficiency. These two were my lodestars, my main principles, because it is not even in my nature to embrace demonstrations of force in front of those who are weaker or to try to intimidate. In those terms, these two men were not really part of the times in which they were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any Defence counsel have questions? Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you related to your statement and a couple of exhibits that were notified to me that might be used in connection with your testimony. In paragraph 5 of your statement you mentioned you sent reports on the work of your section to the Supreme Command Staff administration for moral guidance. Who was the -- who was the person in charge at the Supreme Command Staff level of the administration for moral guidance in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since I was at a forward command post accompanying my commander, General Pavkovic, there were four or five relocations. The command post was in Nis. There were two officers at the command post as reinforcement from the administration for morale from the General Staff of Serbia and Montenegro. Professionally, my superior was Mr. Bakocevic later major-general, and his deputy. Through combat reports we provided reports from the forward command post reflecting all important developments that took place in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, namely, the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army. Just one more thing, if I may add. In mid-April 1999 there was a team from the administration for information and morale conducting a study of morale among the troops of the 3rd Army, focusing on the Pristina Corps. There were five or six persons on that team. In May there was another group of officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard some testimony about that from a couple of other witnesses. The question I was trying to get is if you know the names of the individuals on the Supreme Command Staff to whom the reports on your report in the 3rd Army were sent? Can you tell us who that would have been?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, through the regular combat reports that the command of the Pristina Corps, and I suppose the 3rd Army as well, the Supreme Command Staff was informed. And in para 6 of a regular combat report always reflected combat activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the last three or four minutes we've been trying to find out if you know the names of the personnel at Supreme Command Staff who would handle your reports. Do you know these names? If you don't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please forgive me, I really didn't know. It was addressed to the Supreme Command Staff, and my controllers were Slobodan Stojanovic, Mile Novkovic, Nedjo Danilovic, and another officer -- there were four officers conducting an inspection and control on my location, I'm more than certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you mentioned being at the forward command post. Were you there throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was that located? What was the physical location? What building? What street address was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the forward command post relocated frequently because of possible attacks by Siptar terrorists and also air-strikes. We were in Grmija, Kisnica, Gracanica. We relocated depending on the risk of being destroyed by those who were keeping us under surveillance. There was nothing certain that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last thing he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer. You said there was nothing certain, and then the interpreter missed the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. Is it anywhere on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's the point, it's not. I had hoped you weren't putting your glasses on so you could hear better. The -- your answer trailed off after you said that you relocated depending on the risk from those keeping you under surveillance. There was nothing certain, and then we didn't hear the rest of your answer. Can you remember what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I repeat. We had no permanent building in which we could say, Here we are at the standing command post of the 3rd Army. That's because there was a constant risk from the Siptar terrorist forces and the NATO air force. We were one of the important targets destined for destruction. We were in Kisnica, Grmija, Gracanica sometimes only for one night. And I guarantee that General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic throughout their working hours continued touring the subordinate units to talk to troops, to inform them, to conduct briefings, and in the afternoons we would meet up to exchange our views on the developments on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, approximately what was the number of personnel that were located in the forward command post of the 3rd Army during the conflict? Are we talking about ten people? A hundred people? A thousand?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Please don't hold it against me, Your Honours, if I can't be sure; but it's 15 to 20. That is the amount of personnel that we moved in as a group in conditions of normal work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We heard from another witness about the operations centre for the 3rd Army command. Do you know where they were located during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The operations centre of the 3rd Army, Mr. Hannis, excuse me, Your Honour. Up to the beginning of air-strikes by the NATO air force on the 4th of April, I believe, the command of the army was bombed and it was located at the command of the army. After that, the operations centre of the 3rd Army was relocated, I don't know where, but I believe that it was to the premises of a private enterprise in Dusanova Street that was a back-up post of the command of the 3rd Army, but I never visited it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of private enterprise it was?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Don't hold me to it. I believe it was some sort of construction company in Obilicev Venac Street, a bit further down the road from the petrol station on the right-hand side. I just have a better visual memory. I could even show you where it was. By sheer accident somebody told me a year later, That's where the operations centre was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave just to add something I think that the witness mentioned how many metres was distance from the -- that building and the building of 3rd Army command. He mentioned, but it is not in transcript, so just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the figure, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 50 [In English] 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 50, 50 metres, 20 and 30. 20 metres from the -- to the petrol station and 30 metres down from the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the 3rd Army command being located in several different locations during the war. You gave us some place names. What kind of buildings was the 3rd Army command housed in in those locations, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I really cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think we're inserting confusion because he was talking about the forward command post of the 3rd Army being located in several locations, not the 3rd Army command. Those are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, maybe I should have said the 3rd Army command and the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that qualification do you understand my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was the forward command post for the 3rd Army located, what type of buildings were they located in those various locations you named earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Beginning with wooden structures, the most primitive ones, to the basic built structured -- structures, brick, and others in Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And similar kinds of structures in the other locations you named or was it only in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Gracanica, Grmija and Kisnica, and Ajvalija, you will excuse me if I can't name them all, it was nine years ago, but it was certainly never in a luxury building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it ever in a school or a private home?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not, I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, Mr. Aleksic asked you about this, the tape-recording that was made to warn people about approaching VJ facility. Do you know, were those audiotapes used in the field?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they announced it from APCs so that people would be acquainted during the war. I have to emphasise there were two stages. There was a temperature emanating from the engine and it created an ideal target for air-strikes by NATO, so it was from October until the 24th of March, and on the 24th of March we stopped this effort for the reason that I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm a little unclear as to when the tape was made. I thought from your earlier answer today you said end of December 1998. And in your written statement --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Mid-December, mid-December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It could be my mistake, in which case I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you didn't have to worry about air-strikes until the 24th of March, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right, but all indications told us that -- you know how the saying goes, better safe than sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But for purposes of how the tape was being used in the field prior to the 24th of March, is it your evidence that these announcements were made from the armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, and also watch-towers, building of military clubs, various buildings, and they were broadcast using a tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any signs posted around military facilities with the same kind of warning, or is it only this oral tape-recording, verbal warning?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: It was a warning that the building was a military installation and it must not be filmed, but the usual pretext they offered was that they could not speak Serbian and they did not understand. That's how those who were caught doing it tried to get out of these accusations. But I knew quite enough, and I tried to protect the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so that's why the audio-recording was made in Albanian as well, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Out of respect for them because it produces a greater effect and it is for preventive purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you answered my earlier question. Were signs also posted with warnings in Serbian and/or Albanian written on them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Sofajlija near the Lukare barracks, I remember the depot of -- explosives depot by which was later hit from an A-10 bomber and for four days there was successive explosions. There were signposts, both in Albanian and the Siptar language saying, Don't approach. So that all the measures were taken prescribed by the law and the army wanted to ensure that it would remain unsoiled before the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention in paragraph 24 of your statement an incident where apparently General Pavkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move to that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are recorded as saying that there were signposts, both in Albanian and the Siptar language, saying, Don't approach. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, in Serbian and in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Listen to me again. You said there were signposts both in the Albanian and the Siptar language saying, Don't approach. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I may have said "Albanian," maybe I said "Siptar." I wanted to say something but -- Your Honour, I was very careful when I was colonel. When I spoke to Albanians I would say to one, You're an Albanian, and he would be insulted, he would find himself offended and say, No, I'm a Siptar. And I would say to another you're a Siptar, and he would say no, no, I'm an Albanian. The name of the country is Siptarije. It's the country of eagles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're misunderstanding my question. I wasn't until this moment aware that there were two separate languages, Albanian and Siptar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to you. The Albanian language is taken from Toska tribe on the south. It's the language of the Albanians, and it's written in the standard Albanian. I apologise to you. So the Albanian standard language is the standard language of the Toska tribe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Not of the Gegaj tribe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So did you have two separate signs in two separate non-Serb languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian and Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do excuse me. I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, in paragraphs 24 and 25 of your statement you make reference to an incident where General Pavkovic dismissed the commander of the 175th Brigade, and in the supplemental information I'm advised that you say he dismissed the commander and his 15 officers from that brigade. First of all, can you tell us when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's mid-April. I may be wrong by a day or two, but it was in mid-April 1992 [as interpreted]. Because of his superficial work, his indisciplined approach to the tasks, the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic, said that he no longer wanted to see either General Petrovic or Drazevic or the 15 officers holding key positions in the 15th brigade. They all handed over their duties. They were all handed over to the VDS or to the military court for processing. And as far as I can recall, Your Honour, around the 15th of May, 1999, Colonel Stojanovic came instead and took over the command, and this unit which did not comply with the image and the idea of the Yugoslav Army, that's why he decided to take this measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you, other than the term you talked about superficial work and indisciplined approach to tasks, do you know anything more specific about why -- why this officer and his 15 other officers were dismissed? What was the specific nature of their shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I said only that because I didn't want to wade into legal waters, but I am aware that in the village of Zegra, some 10 kilometres to the north of Gnjilane, in that same 175th Brigade, something was done which is below the dignity of members of the Army of Yugoslavia. There was a man called Zmajevic, who had a criminal mind, and General Lazarevic heard about it only later on. I think that was the straw that broke the camel's back. Respecting General Pavkovic as an exceptional man, an artist, he said on one occasion, Don't let me be the one to kill the criminal; let the court do it. I remember that very well. When I heard him say that, I understood that it was about something very serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't really know? Because if you do, please tell us -- please tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the specific event. I just read about it. I read about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, according to what you read, can you tell us anything more specific than it was something below the dignity of members of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from what I was able to read, and I will paraphrase, somebody burst into a house and killed an elderly man and an elderly woman. Three men entered the yard of some Albanians, attempted to open the door, were not successful, shot at the door with automatic rifles, and from that group headed by Zmajevic, three persons killed three Albanians. I learned about this a year and a half ago from the White Book, which I read in order to see what crimes had been perpetrated on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija by members of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you refer to the White Book, are you talking about a Vojska publication about how the --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The Official Gazette, Mr. Hannis, the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Not Vojska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me, are you talking about two separate killings here, the killing of an elderly man and an elderly woman and then the killing of three Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm referring to one single day when in a short space of time seven military conscripts did things in the village of Zegra. So it was a brief period of time and a brief territory -- a small territory where seven members committed that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to the brigade commander and his 15 officers, do you know was anything done other than dismissing them? Was there any kind of prosecution against them or were they just dismissed from their positions? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I know that of the 15th or the 14th Colonel Petrovic left, Djurasevic left with him, how I really don't know. I asked the prosecutor to tell me so that I could release information or when going to the subordinate units I could draw attention to the consequences, but he said to me, My ethics does not allow me to tell you that, the proceedings are not over, the investigation is not over. When it's all over, we will deliver it to you so that you can inform your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the prosecutor that told you that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Djuro Blagojevic, captain first class, I think it was him. I'm 90 per cent sure it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you an exhibit, it's number 3D732. I can give you a hard copy and ask you: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an aide-memoire. The author is Colonel Dr. Petar Kostic, and it's guide-lines for troop psychologists in a brigade or regiment in a state of war. He is a professor in the military academy at Banjica, he is the author of several books, and to the best of my knowledge this is almost the first time he dealt with the war. He had enormous theoretical knowledge and he wanted to use that and the practical combat experience he had gained as a volunteer in the 175th Infantry Brigade looking at all the manifestations on the faces of soldiers and their body language after throwing hand-grenades. He interviewed them, and based on these interviews and based on their grimaces, he wrote instructions, guide-lines, with a view to having people not experience what he had experienced and for people in the units to find it easier to recognise fear and all the other elements that have a destructive effect on morale. So that in practical terms, Mr. Hannis, this is combat experience couched in theoretical terms so that future generations in military schools and academies could learn from this experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, the cover document is dated the 29th of May, 1999, and this is from you forwarding those guide-lines, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it sometime before the 29th of May you had these guide-lines. Did you read them? Did you review them before you sent them out?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read it before sending it out, but the commander -- the commands of the independent battalions and the commands of units of the same rank are not duty-bound, are not obliged to respond to this document. They may keep the guide-lines to use, and after proposed changes arrived, the material offered by units brigade regiment size the final version of the guide-lines will be drafted and delivered to all the units. So this is one of the possible versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. We saw from another witness I think a more final version, but my question is: Did you agree with these proposals?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Conditionally -- in my, conditionally speaking, workbook up to the beginning of the war, that is, I kept a workbook. After the beginning of the war on receiving orders from either General Lazarevic or General Pavkovic, on a scrap of paper, a small scrap of paper, I entered small, short messages of encoded as to what should be done in subordinate units. And the reason for that was if I was caught or captured by Siptar terrorists, they could find nothing except that small scrap of paper on me. If I had had a workbook on me, they would see the whole history of what I had done while I was at the forward command post. I enter data which was left with the typist, with all that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I don't -- I'm not following that this is anything to do with your question, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's beyond that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about on the last page, sir, item number 2 is tasks and methodologies of work depending on the participants, and you see something called: "Form of addressing the combatants." Do you see that on the last page?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's page 5. Is it the fifth page? Is it page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
