utterances.text: I believe it's the last page in your bundle and it's highlighted in pink --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: The last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. Do you see that? And do you see a section highlighted in the colour pink? Yes. And this appears to be a scenario where a commander is dealing with combatants, some of whom are refusing to participate. And it talks about dealing with those who temporarily cannot do the task but want to, those who permanently cannot but want to, and those who don't want to. And in the end he proposes that they be told: "Therefore, there are only three places where the conscripts can be: At the combat positions; in the courtroom, prison; or in an asylum. Help me choose." So did you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I rejected that. I wrote down: This is out of the question, because in my assessment these people cannot carry weapons and the madhouse is out of the question. An asylum is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 28 of your statement you tell us about some problems VJ encountered in mid-May when the 7th -- I think it's the 7th Partisan Brigade had large-scale desertions, do you recall that, or the 7th Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, don't hold it against me, but let me ask you something. The 7th Brigade had more deserters, 2.248 men, that was 48 per cent, but that was on the 18th and 19th of May, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just reading from your statement where it says "mid-May."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, 18th or 19th of May, 1999, there were more desertions. And the then-commander, General Pavkovic, but also General Lazarevic because the two acted as one, they tasked me with establishing the reasons for this. And later on a team from the General Staff, including the morale administration, sent two people to establish the causes of the desertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you that. Your statement says: "The order was to attempt to prevent them from leaving, but to let those who wanted to leave go without taking any repressive measures." What did you do? What did you do to try and prevent them from leaving?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before leaving I asked General Pavkovic, saying as there's a state of war -- I asked him what measures I would be allowed to use. And he said to me, Old man - excuse me, that's what he called me - he said, Old man, who has decided to leave, well good luck to him. But he -- how will he be able to say later on that he left the battle-field of Kosovo? They successively came back. A very small number came back, but the reputation of the Serbian army was besmirched, it was soiled. The reasons, because I spent four days and four nights there talking to people, and if time allows and if you allow, I'm willing to tell you. I will need about three minutes for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing you said there was that they successively came back, a very small number came back. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A large number came back, but a small number remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point I wish to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, on page 78 of the record lines 9 and 10, you said: "Professionally my superior in the General Staff was -- he later became General Bakocevic did I understand you correctly that the chief of administration for morale was General Bakocevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On page 79 lines 9 and 10 you said the four people from the administration for morale came only to visit, they were not superior commanders, it was General Bakocevic who was the chief of the administration for morale?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO STARCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a small digression to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, that was quite enough, quite sufficient. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Starcevic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give evidence to us. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought Mr. Ackerman would raise this issue. Well, anyway, unfortunately we don't have a witness for these last ten minutes because we -- well, the witness is in town but we have not succeeded with the Victims and Witnesses Unit to organize his arrival in the court on time. You can deduct these ten minutes from our time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the next witness Zarko Kostic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the next witness is Stanimir Radosavljevic. We sent notification over the weekend that there would be a change in the order of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall resume at 2.15, 2.15, tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of October, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.36 p.m.,
